summary:
Allwork.Space reports, citing The Wall Street Journal, that nearly 1 in 5 online job advertisements may never lead to a hire. Data from hiring platform Greenhouse classified roughly 19% of jobs advertised on digital job boards in the second quarter as "ghost jobs," defined as postings that received at least one application but generated no hiring activity such as interviews or job tests. Employers keep such listings live for several reasons: building a pipeline of future candidates, pausing hiring after posting, or deciding to fill the role internally.

Lawmakers are responding. New York passed legislation requiring employers to state when advertised positions are expected to be filled and to remove listings once filled, with fines for violations. In Pennsylvania, a bill from state Rep. Jim Prokopiak would require accurate hiring plan information and timelines for removing postings. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has opened an investigation into LinkedIn over whether its job listings mislead users about genuine opportunities. LinkedIn responded that its policies require postings to be authentic and accurately represented, and noted that some listings display employer response times and whether candidates are being reviewed.

The article illustrates job seeker frustration through Heather Sanford, an Austin-area marketing professional who says she has applied to more than 3,000 jobs since her contract ended in May 2025 and has seen roles reposted after no response.

Ghost jobs also distort labor market data. The Labor Department's definition of a job opening requires active recruiting for a role that could begin within 30 days, so ghost listings are excluded from official figures. Economic uncertainty compounds the issue: employers may pause approved roles, reconsider external hiring, or fill positions internally, leaving stale postings online.

The piece does not address workplace operations topics such as desk booking, visitor management, or return-to-office policy.
